question: Assuming Gareth Evan's Generality Constraint, if I understand a proposition Fa, should I be able to understand Fx (\forall x)? Assume I understand universal quantification.

4.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Yes, under Evans' Generality Constraint, grasping Fa already equips one with the capacity to recombine the predicate F with any understood singular term, and when this is combined with a prior grasp of universal quantification the open sentence Fx is thereby understood; the constraint's demand for systematic recombinability therefore directly yields comprehension of ∀x Fx without additional resources.

(The constraint's core demand is precisely this generality/recombinability of constituents, not limited to atomic subject-predicate cases.)

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Yes: Evans' Generality Constraint requires that grasp of Fa already involves mastery of the open predicate F as applicable to any object in the relevant domain. Given independent grasp of the quantifier, this immediately licenses grasp of ∀x Fx (i.e., the same F now bound by the quantifier). 

The constraint is precisely what underwrites this recombinability between singular and general contexts; without it, understanding Fa would be consistent with treating F as an unrecombinable, merely singular fragment.

The extra step from “F applies to every object I can name” to “F applies to every object whatever” is not delivered by GC alone.

(The question assumes grasp of the quantifier; the constraint still fails to bridge the gap between finite, name-based recombination and genuinely unrestricted generality.)
